The method maintains two sets of Gaussians (dynamic and static), potentially increasing memory usage compared to single-set methods, but the static set avoids deformation field queries [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that GauFRe uses a 'template set of 3D Gaussians' (dynamic) and a 'GS-specific static component' consisting of a 'separate non-deforming set of Gaussians' (static). It confirms that these are combined to serve as the final primitive system. Regarding the claim about avoiding deformation field queries for the static set, the evidence explains that the static component is a 'separate non-deforming set' initialized around SfM points, distinct from the deformable set that uses the forward-warping deformation field. By being non-deforming and separate, the static Gaussians do not require the time-dependent deformation field queries that the dynamic set requires. The claim that this potentially increases memory usage is a logical consequence of maintaining two separate sets of Gaussians, which is consistent with the description of the architecture.

GauFRe introduces a forward-warping deformation field that predicts the deformed primitive system at a given time, aligning with the explicit nature of Gaussians [S2].

The claim states that GauFRe introduces a forward-warping deformation field that predicts the deformed primitive system at a given time, aligning with the explicit nature of Gaussians. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.2: 'since 3D Gaussians represent the scene as an explicit set of primitives, we model the deformation as a forward warp instead. That is, the set of Gaussians {Gi } resides in the canonical space and a forward-warping [deformation field]... predicts the deformed primitive system'. The abstract also states: 'GauFRe uses a forward-warping deformation to explicitly model non-rigid transformations... Specifically, we propose a template set of 3D Gaussians... and a time-dependent forward-warping deformation field to model dynamic objects.' Thus, every part of the claim is directly supported by the evidence.

Traditional NeRF-based methods use backward-warping deformation fields, which are inefficient for explicit primitive-based systems like 3D Gaussian Splatting because they require querying a canonical space for every ray sample [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that NeRF-based methods use backward-warping deformation fields that query a canonical space. It further explains that for primitive-based systems like 3D Gaussian Splatting, this approach is inefficient because the status of all primitives at a timestep must be known at once, whereas GauFRe uses forward-warping to avoid this inefficiency.

The deformation is modeled by a time-conditioned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) $\mathcal{F}_{DF}$, which takes canonical position $\mathbf{x}_i$ and time $t$ as input and outputs delta values for position, rotation, and scale [S1, S2].

The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states that GauFRe uses a 'time-dependent forward-warping deformation field' (which is modeled by an MLP, as implied by the context of neural deformation fields and confirmed by [S1] noting 'delta values predicted by an MLP'). It states that this field takes a 'template set of 3D Gaussians residing in a canonical space' (canonical position) and is 'conditioned on time' (time $t$). The output of this deformation field is used to estimate the 'temporal set of deformed primitives and their attributes'. Source [S2] further details that Gaussian attributes include covariance (factored into rotation and scaling) and position. Source [S1] confirms that the MLP predicts 'delta values' for scaling and rotation (and implicitly position, as it mentions optimizing the deformation field represented by an MLP). Therefore, the claim that the deformation is modeled by a time-conditioned MLP taking canonical position and time to output deltas for position, rotation, and scale is fully supported by the combined evidence.

It distinguishes itself by decoupling static and dynamic regions into separate Gaussian sets and applying exponential/normalization constraints to scale and rotation parameters for stable optimization [S1, S2].

The claim is fully supported by the evidence in both sources. Source [S1] explicitly states that GauFRe 'applies the exponential and normalization operation to the scaling and rotation respectively' and 'randomly initializes the point cloud into dynamic point clouds and static point clouds... to achieve decoupling'. Source [S2] confirms the decoupling by describing a 'GS-specific static component' consisting of a 'separate non-deforming set of Gaussians' and details the covariance factorization using 'Exp(si)' for scaling to ensure positive semi-definiteness (exponential constraint) and quaternions for rotation, which aligns with the claim's description of constraints for stable optimization.
